verses.text: I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as confirmed by my conscience in the Holy Spirit.
I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.
For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood,
the people of Israel. Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises.
Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.
It is not as though God's word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.
Nor because they are Abraham's descendants are they all his children. On the contrary, "Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned."
So it is not the children of the flesh who are God's children, but it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring.
For this is what the promise stated: "At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son."
Not only that, but Rebecca's children were conceived by one man, our father Isaac.
Yet before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God's plan of election might stand,
not by works but by Him who calls, she was told, "The older will serve the younger."
So it is written: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not!
For He says to Moses: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion."
So then, it does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy.
For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: "I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden.
One of you will say to me, "Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?"
But who are you, O man, to talk back to God? Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it, "Why did You make me like this?"
Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?
What if God, intending to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction?
What if He did this to make the riches of His glory known to the vessels of His mercy, whom He prepared in advance for glory—
including us, whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?
As He says in Hosea: "I will call them 'My People' who are not My people, and I will call her 'My Beloved' who is not My beloved,"
and, "It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not My people,' they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.
For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively."
It is just as Isaiah foretold: "Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah."
What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith;
but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it.
Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
as it is written: "See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame."

context.author: Paul the apostle, writing through a secretary named Tertius (1:1; 16:22)
context.genre: Letter (epistle), written as a carefully argued case for the gospel
context.audience: The Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles
context.setting: Paul begins with deep grief for his own people, the Israelites, who have so many privileges but have mostly not believed. He then explains that God’s promise has not failed, because it was never based on physical descent. He walks through God’s choice of Isaac, Jacob, and Pharaoh, and the calling of Gentiles.
context.custom: Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges (vv.4-5) comes from what Jews took pride in: adoption, glory, covenants, the law, worship, promises, and the patriarchs. The image of a potter and clay (vv.20-21) was a common picture of God’s power.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 10 balances this by showing human responsibility, since Israel did not submit to God’s righteousness. Chapter 11 shows that God has not rejected Israel.
context.timelineBible: Paul quotes Genesis 21:12 (Isaac), Genesis 18:10, Malachi 1:2-3 (Jacob and Esau), Exodus 33:19 and 9:16 (Moses and Pharaoh), Hosea 1-2, and Isaiah 10:22 and 28:16.
context.sparkNotes: Paul wishes he could be cut off for his people’s sake. He explains that God’s promise follows his own call, not descent, with examples from Abraham’s family and Pharaoh. He says God shows mercy as he chooses, and that Gentiles have now been called while many in Israel stumbled over the stone.

translation.meaning: Choosing, selection. Paul uses it for God’s purpose in choosing, not for human merit.
Compassion shown to people in need and not deserving. The word is central to the chapter.

otBackground.note: “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be reckoned.”
“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.”
The stone laid in Zion, which is a stumbling block or a foundation.

overview.summary: Paul grieves for Israel and argues that God’s promise stands because it rests on his calling, not on birth. God’s mercy now reaches Gentiles, while many in Israel have stumbled.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Corinth to the Christians in Rome.

history.t: The adoption, the covenants and the law are listed as real privileges (vv.4-5).
Isaiah’s “remnant” is a small group that stays faithful, a pattern Paul says holds now.

customs.t: The firstborn son normally got the larger inheritance. God reversed that for Jacob and Esau.
Potters were common in towns, and Jeremiah 18 uses the image of clay shaped by the potter.

archaeology.t: Excavated workshops in Jerusalem and Corinth show the scale of the trade.
Egyptian records of Pharaohs show the setting for the exodus story Paul quotes.

overview.discussion: Paul’s words here are among the hardest in the Bible. What do I do with a passage that I don’t fully understand, and how can I read it with humility?
overview.book: The letter to the Romans · 16 chapters. Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel, written to a church he had not yet visited.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: Esau Selling His Birthright, by Hendrick ter Brugghen (about 1625). Romans 9:10-13 recalls Jacob and Esau to show that God's choice rests on his call.

currentImage.caption: A clay plaque from Penteskouphia, near Corinth, showing potters at a kiln (about the 6th century BC). It is Greek, not Judean, but it shows the craft behind Paul's picture of the potter and the clay (Romans 9:21).
